rationale: A wins because it is the steadier press instrument: it keeps the launch facts in view and tells the founder exactly what proof would make each lane real. Its strongest line, "Educators Say Duolingo Is Gamified Fluff. Its Users Are Spending Nine Minutes on AI Conversations," has a clean adversary and an honest proof burden. B is sharper in places, but "Duolingo says people are talking to its cartoon owl for nine minutes at a time" invents from the supplied facts, and cute-but-wrong is how pitches die in public.
gaps_in_A: "Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence" smuggles causality; the update gives growth and profitability, not proof that one explains the other.
"Why Duolingo Made Chess Free and AI Tutoring Expensive" overstates two facts: Max is paid, not proven expensive, and Lily video calls are conversation practice, not a tutoring product.
"clearest signal yet that Duolingo sees itself as more than a language product" needs an executive quote or broader product context; with only one chess course, the platform thesis is thin.

"whether it can replace a human tutor" is a useful provocation, but the update gives no pricing, outcome, or tutor-comparison evidence, so it must stay a reporting question, not the pitch's implied claim.
gaps_in_B: "cartoon owl" is not in the update; the supplied character is Lily. That factual shortcut would get corrected before it got covered.
"9 minutes per session in beta is a long time for a voice interaction in a mobile app" declares the comparison before establishing a baseline; the proof section knows this, the angle should too.
"expensive AI feature" goes beyond the supplied fact that Max is paid; no price, margin, or cost evidence is given.
"No urgent hook" and "the set has no current news signal anchoring it" underrate the actual simultaneous launch peg. The peg may be thin, but it exists.
